atha caturtho vimarśaḥ | prasṛtamanuttararūpādānandādikrameṇa viśvamadaḥ | sarvāmṛtadharamantarbahiśca visṛjantamabhivande || jñānakriyādhikārayugalena tattvārthasaṅgrahasahitena svaprakāśe'pi tattve yuktyupabṛṃhite nirūpite svataḥ ityaṃśaḥ pūritaḥ āgamādhikāreṇa, tameva arthamupodbalayatā śāstrataḥ iti ayam | śāstradṛṣṭirapi tatprasiddhaguruparamparopadeśena samyagāgamatvaṃ neyā | yathā uktaṃ prāk śāmbhavanītyādīnāmapi ityādi | tata eva paramahadantarāladivyadivyādivyādivyasambandhamanādṛtya sbuddhipustakamātraśaraṇā viḍambitā ityāśayena pustakādhītavidyāśca gurukramavivarjitāḥ | ācaranto diśantaśca pacyante narake ciram || yātanārājarājānāṃ te bhoktāro vininditāḥ | tasmādgurukramāyātaṃ diśanneti paraṃ śivam || iti uktam | tato gurutaḥ iti ayaṃ tṛtīyaḥ aṃśaḥ pūrayitavyaḥ | uktaṃ hi śrīkiraṇāyāṃ ---------------------------gurutaḥ śāstrataḥ svataḥ | iti | tamaṃśaṃ pūrayituṃ ślokatrayeṇa prakārāntaramāha | tatra prathamaślokena svaguruparvakramaṃ vadannādiśrīkaṇṭhanāthāt pravṛttimasya darśayati upadeśasya apūrvatvena aprayāsakāritvena avaśyopadeśyatāṃ ca | dvitīyena abhijñānaprakaṭanātmanā upadeśaḥ sato'pi asatkalpasya anuprāṇakaḥ iti tatra ādaraḥ kartavyaḥ iti darśitam | tṛtīyena vyākhyānaśravaṇacintanābhyasanasāphalyasiddhaye svakapūrvaguruvandanamavaśyaṃ kartavyamiti śikṣayā pravṛttaśiṣyānugrahāya svātmano gurutve yogyatābhidhānāya (page 401) kīrtanīyo gurorvargaḥ śāstrārthasya prasiddhaye | itinayaṃ pālayituṃ pituralaukikavastuviṣayaprasiddhyabhidhānena upakārāya prasiddho diṣṭe lokaḥ pravartate | iti lokasya apravṛttasya pravartanādvāreṇa ca anugrahāya ca svātmano vaṃśapradarśanapūrvakanāmaprakaṭīkaraṇapuraḥsaramadhikāraprayoja- nasambandhābhidheyābhidhānānāṃ nigamanamiti prakaraṇārthaḥ | pratiślokaṃ tu artho nirūpaṇīyaḥ | saca spaṣṭa eva, vṛttivivṛtyośca nirūpitaḥ | yattu kiñcit kiñcidaspaṣṭamatra, tadeva vimṛśyate iti prakaṭito mayā sughaṭa eṣa mārgo navo mahāgurubhirucyate
**The closing sum: the recognition, and the end of the whole teaching** We come to the end. This final vimarśa of the Īśvarapratyabhijñāvivṛtivimarśinī is the closing sum — the drawing together of everything that has gone before. And its theme is fittingly the *transmission* of the teaching itself: it comes from the guru, from the śāstra, and from the self. The whole teaching — the self-manifest essence, established by the knowledge and the action, aided by reason — has been given. Part of it comes from the self (svataḥ); part from the śāstra (śāstrataḥ); and part must come from the guru (gurutaḥ). For even the vision of the śāstra must be carried to its proper power by the lineage of teachers. And here Abhinavagupta is stern: "the book-studied knowledges, without the guru-order," he warns, "practicing and teaching, ripen long in hell." The teaching must be received from the living line — from the ādi-Śrīkaṇṭhanātha down through Durvāsa and Tryambakāditya, the mental sons who carry the un-precedented, effort-less word. And now the path itself. Abhinavagupta presents it as a "new, well-fitted path," spoken by the great gurus in the Śivadṛṣṭi. It is the path of the recognition. Since liberation is from the recognition alone, all the elaborate effort-yogas are useless here; this is the clear means, effort-less, un-undertaken, yet bearing the great fruit. The breath-controls and the rest are artificial; the un-made reality does not yield to a sixteenth part of such effort. Even the proud fancies of the bound — "I am the king," "I have slain my enemy" — are, when examined, still other-dependent, riding on the Lord's power. The recognition cuts through all of it. And its fruit is the while-living-liberated, the jīvanmukta: the one who, even in the body, is already free, and who at the fall of the body is simply the supreme Lord. This, Abhinavagupta says, is the most wondrous thing of all — liberation in this very life. The closing sum puts it in a beautiful image. The lover stands near, sought by the slender woman; but as long as he is not recognized, he cannot be enjoyed. So the world-Lord — always present, always near — is not experienced in his own splendor until the recognition arises. The world has him before it, and yet does not see him, until the single act of recognition turns the un-known nearness into the joy of union. One who knows only the mere flash of recognition gains the bliss; one who cultivates it gains the thousand-fold embrace. And this recognition, Abhinavagupta reminds us, was established for the world by Utpala — "the sun-rise son" — for the effort-less establishment of all people, not by caste or conduct but by the very fact of being born a knower. Through it, all beings are graced; and by it, the author himself is complete. The whole teaching — the Lord's recognition — is here gathered and handed on. The closing vimarśa then turns to the author's own lineage — the vivṛtikāra's seventeen verses of praise. They trace the line: Varāha-gupta, the Cukhulaka, father of Bhūtirāja; Bhūtirāja himself; Haṭitalakṣmaṇagupta, the maker of the śāstra, the guru of Abhinava; the Tryambaka with its three powers; and the method of the recognition throughout. The final verses praise the supreme Lord and hand the work to him: "the Lord-recognition, from the reflective-awareness of the Lord, may he make it the one minding the self's reflection." And then the two colophons close the entire work: the "all-conclusion, the fourth vimarśa"; and "completed — this, the Īśvarapratyabhijñāvivṛtivimarśinī, the composition of the Abhinavagupta-foots, whose fame is won by meditation on the feet of Tri-nayana." So ends the greatest work of Abhinavagupta — the Vivṛtivimarśinī on the recognition of the Lord. It has traced, across four adhikāras, the knowledge and the action of consciousness, the categories of the world, the knowers and the stains, the bond and the liberation. > The closing sum of the IPVV. The teaching comes from the self, the śāstra, and the guru; the > book-studied knowledge without the guru-order is sterile. And its path is the recognition: since > liberation is from the recognition alone, the elaborate effort-yogas are useless here; this is the > clear means, effort-less, yet bearing the great fruit. Its fruit is the jīvanmukta — the one > liberated while still living. > > The lover-image states how this is so. The lover stands near, sought by the slender woman, but as > long as he is not recognized, he cannot be enjoyed. So the world-Lord, always present, always near, > is not experienced in his own splendor until the recognition arises. Recognition does not bring the > Lord; it turns the un-known nearness into the joy of union. And because the recognition is an event > to be occasioned, not a proposition to be believed, the teaching must come from the guru — the book > without the line is sterile. > > The passage establishes the recognition as the path and the jīvanmukta as its fruit.
